endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: Clinicians should be a ware of the risks of patients engaging with generative AI products that produce inaccurate or harmful medical information (e.g., patients asking chatbots about symptoms) and should be prepared to counsel patients on the limitations of AI-driven medical advice.

endorsements.title: Large language models could change the future of behavioral healthcare: a proposal for responsible development and evaluation
endorsements.quote: However, LLMs are advancing quickly and will soon be deployed in the clinical domain, with little oversight or understanding of harms that they may produce. While cautious optimism about clinical LLM applications is warranted, it is also crucial for psychologists to approach the integration of LLMs into psychotherapy with caution and to educate the public about the potential risks and limitations of using these technologies for therapeutic purposes.

endorsements.title: Delusional Experiences Emerging From AI Chatbot Interactions or "AI Psychosis"
endorsements.quote: Psychotherapeutic interventions could include psychoeducation on digital reality testing, helping patients to identify when online or AI-mediated interactions begin to shape beliefs in maladaptive ways.

endorsements.title: Considerations about the proliferation of large language model chatbots and youth mental health
endorsements.quote: It seems that mental health professionals have a role to play in education on the likely limitations of common LLMs for mental health support, and a potential need for AI LLM use screening in some contexts (Hudon and Stip 2025).

endorsements.title: Generative AI as a de facto mental health provider: a policy brief and urgent call for regulation
endorsements.quote: Guide Patients Toward Digital-Mental Literacy: Help patients understand both the potential benefits (e.g., initial accessibility) and the significant risks of using AI for mental health.

endorsements.title: Artificial intelligence-assisted mental healthcare in general practice: Benefits, risks and future possibilities
endorsements.quote: Educating patients about the tool’s purpose and limitations is also critical to set appropriate expectations.

endorsements.title: A strategic pathway for the ethical development of AI tools in dementia care
endorsements.issuer: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association
endorsements.quote: They are expected to explain the purpose, benefits, risks, and limitations of these technologies to patients and caregivers – just as they do with traditional medical interventions.

endorsements.title: The Patient-AI Relationship in Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders: A Cognitive-Behavioral Framework
endorsements.quote: Patients may benefit from understanding that LLMs are optimized for user satisfaction, are prone to agreeing with the user’s framing [ 32 ], and can generate convincing inaccuracies.

evidence.title: Large Language Models as Health Information Tools: Patient Use and Trust in Otolaryngology
evidence.outcome: Patient use of consumer LLM chatbots for health information before clinic visit
evidence.effect: 71.2% reported prior LLM use, and 28.6% used an LLM to learn about their condition before the visit; 93.8% did not disclose it to clinicians.
evidence.quote: Among 59 respondents (mean age 50.1 years; 53.4% female), 71.2% reported prior LLM use, and 28.6% used an LLM to learn about their condition before the visit.

evidence.title: Bias and Inaccuracy in AI Chatbot Ophthalmologist Recommendations
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of consumer chatbot recommendations of ophthalmologists (specialty and location correctness)
evidence.effect: Inaccurate recommendations: ChatGPT 73.8%, Bing Chat 67.5%, Bard 62.5%; most recommendations were non-ophthalmologists or not in or near the desired city.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT (73.8%), Bing Chat (67.5%), and Bard (62.5%) gave high rates of inaccurate recommendations.
evidence.sample_unit: chatbot ophthalmologist recommendations (80 per chatbot x 3 chatbots)

evidence.title: ChatGPT-4o-Generated Exercise Plans for Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus-Assessment of Their Safety and Other Quality Criteria by Coaching Experts
evidence.effect: Across nine plans for three T2DM profiles, authors concluded the plans were not fully safe, especially for secondary diseases/complications.
evidence.quote: Our results imply that ChatGPT-4o-generated exercise plans are not (yet) fully safe for patients with T2DM, especially not for those with secondary diseases/complications.

evidence.title: Clinical Failure of General-Purpose AI in Photographic Scoliosis Assessment: A Diagnostic Accuracy Study
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy of general-purpose LLMs assessing scoliosis from photographs versus radiographic reference
evidence.effect: ChatGPT specificity 0% (95% CI 0.0-14.8), misclassifying all non-AIS cases; Claude 2 78.3% false positives; ChatGPT thoracic Cobb overestimated by +10.74° (LoA -21.45° to +42.92°).
evidence.quote: The LLMs exhibited hazardous diagnostic inaccuracy: ChatGPT misclassified all non-AIS cases (specificity 0% [95% CI: 0.0-14.8]), while Claude 2 generated 78.3% false positives.
evidence.sample_unit: adolescents (74 with AIS, 23 with postural asymmetry)

commentary.bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether clinician counseling about consumer chatbots changes how patients use chatbot advice or whether it prevents harm. Support comes from five endorsements, four of them commentaries, and from four studies that document inaccurate chatbot output and low patient disclosure of chatbot use.

perspectives.view: No supplied study tests clinician counseling on consumer chatbots. The four hazard studies are cross-sectional, vignette, or simulated designs, three rated level 4. They show that inaccurate chatbot output occurs, but they do not show that counseling reduces patient reliance or harm. Four of the five endorsements are commentaries, so the recommendation rests mainly on expert opinion.

Inaccurate output appeared across different tasks. Between 62.5% and 73.8% of chatbot ophthalmologist recommendations were wrong. ChatGPT showed 0% specificity for scoliosis on photographs. Exercise plans for type 2 diabetes were judged not fully safe. These studies describe the failure mode, and none tests whether counseling catches such errors before patients act on them.

In one clinic survey of 59 patients, 28.6% used an LLM to learn about their condition before the visit, and 93.8% did not disclose it. This suggests clinicians may not know when counseling is needed unless they ask directly. No study reports how such questions fit into visit workflow or how much time they add.

None of the hazard studies reports enrolling Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy participants, and one study did not report its country. The supplied evidence cannot show whether counseling would reach these patients as well as others, or whether chatbot errors affect them differently.

Most surveyed patients who used chatbots did not tell their clinicians, which suggests clinicians may need to start the conversation. Counseling could give patients a person to check chatbot advice with. No study has measured its effect on patient trust, disclosure, or access to a human clinician.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares structured clinician counseling about consumer chatbots with usual care. A trial or pragmatic evaluation should measure patient disclosure of chatbot use, reliance on chatbot advice, harmful actions taken, and visit time. It should enroll patients across literacy levels and languages and include safety-net settings.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tests the practice. None of the four hazard studies reports including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, so the evidence gives no basis for judging whether counseling would work for these groups or whether they face different chatbot risks.
